newsitem.title: USA: Heating oil drops sharply as stocks build.
newsitem.headline: Heating oil drops sharply as stocks build.

text.p: Heating oil prices fell sharply on Wednesday after a weekly report on inventories showed a large rise in available stocks and set off a round of selling by speculators who had bet that supplies would remain tight.
At the New York Mercantile Exchange, November heating oil fell 2.22 cents a gallon to close at 73.97 cents.
Heating oil stocks in the United States remain 17 million barrels below a year ago, a fact that has pushed heating oil futures to the highest levels since January, 1991.

But in weekly statistics released late on Tuesday, the American Petroleum Institute (API) reported distillate stocks, which include heating oil, grew by 1.3 million barrels for the latest week. Traders had been expecting a much smaller build.
"The data may have given the feeling that we have turned the corner," said Refco Energy Group vice president Victor Yu.
"The dam finally broke. People decided to take profits while they can," said Al Lindseth, a trader with GSC Energy.
The sell-off in heating oil also took crude oil lower with November crude oil ending down 47 cents a barrel at $25.07.

Selling in crude oil picked up after U.N. Under Secretary General Chinmaya Gharekhan said he was trying to get visas for three oil monitors from the Dutch-based Saybolt firm to go to Iraq under the pending Iraqi oil-for-food plan.
But, he also said minimum conditions had still not been met to implement the plan.

Under a deal with the U.N. agreed in May, Iraq was to be allowed to sell $2 billion worth of oil over six months to buy food, medicine and other humanitarian aid. That deal was frozen when Iraqi troops moved into Kurdistan in late August.
Iraq, potentially a leading oil exporter, has been under stiff U.N. economic sanctions since the 1991 Gulf War.
November gasoline ended 0.91 cent a gallon lower at 65.59 cents, shadowing the drop in heating oil.
But traders noted that gasoline stocks fell in the latest API report due to seasonal maintenance of refineries, a factor that could work to support prices in coming days.
In other markets, Chicago Board of Trade wheat futures rose as worries about delayed seeding of winter wheat in the eastern Corn Belt sparked buying by speculators.
Wheat for delivery in July 1997, which will see the first delivery of the crop planted this fall, rose 5-1/4 cents a bushel at $3.77.

The late maturation of the soybean crop in the eastern Corn Belt led to the talk of late wheat planting. A significant portion of wheat in that area is grown on land also used for soybeans, which were planted late due to a wet spring.
"There is a concern that they (farmers) won't be able to plant their wheat on time," said James Beuerlein, extension agronomist at Ohio State University.
The Agriculture Department on Monday said the wheat seeding pace in Ohio, Indiana and Illinois were well behind the year-ago and average pace for this time of year.

December corn closed 2-3/4 cents a bushel lower at $2.93-3/4 on the outlook for a bumper nine-billion-bushel crop this fall. November soybeans rose 1-3/4 cents at $7.38-1/4 cents per bushel, with concerns about cold Midwest weather delaying harvest or hurting yields.
At the Coffee Cocoa and Sugar Exchange in New York, cocoa futures closed higher as surprisingly strong German demand touched off buying by speculators.
December cocoa closed up $18 a metric ton at $1,385.

German cocoa grindings rose by seven percent in the third quarter 1996 to 65,824 tonnes. Germany's strong demand came on the heels of sharply higher grindings reported earlier in the United Kingdom and the Netherlands last quarter, traders said.
